comments.author: @EdwardThatch-ee7yx
comments.text:
Slavery was abolished in Mauritius on 1st February 1835 under British colonial rule, following the British Parliament’s Slavery Abolition Act of 1833. However, this freedom came at a considerable cost to the newly emancipated population: the British Government paid approximately £2.1 million in compensation to the Franco-Mauritian slave owners (equivalent to approximately £346.3 million in 2026). The formerly enslaved people received no compensation for their suffering or years of forced labour. They were also subjected to an apprenticeship system (further slavery) that required them to continue working for their former owners, which ended in Mauritius in 1839.

Britain played the leading role in the international campaign against slavery. Parliament abolished the British slave trade in 1807 and slavery throughout most of the British Empire through the 1833 Act, with emancipation taking effect in 1834 and subsequent years. The Royal Navy also conducted anti-slave-trade patrols. These were significant contributions to abolition.

Le Morne Brabant, in southwestern Mauritius, became a refuge for enslaved people who escaped their captors and lived as maroons in its caves and on its summit. Today, the mountain stands as a powerful symbol of resistance, suffering and the struggle for freedom.

According to a well-known Mauritian oral tradition, when British authorities arrived to announce the abolition of slavery, some maroons feared that the soldiers had come to recapture them. The story says that they chose to leap to their deaths rather than face enslavement again. However, this dramatic account has not been conclusively established as historical fact, and UNESCO acknowledges the legend as part of the mountain’s cultural heritage.

Le Morne remains a place of remembrance and a symbol of the courage and resistance of those who fought for freedom. Its cultural landscape was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2008, and the legacy of slavery and emancipation continues to be commemorated in Mauritius.
